questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.learningObjective: state that an invariant constrains every observable state, not only the state the constructor leaves
questions.stem: A booth class states one invariant: at most one of leftOpen and rightOpen is true, and the constructor starts with both false. A client then calls openLeft() and later openRight(). What does the invariant oblige the class to do?

options.text: Keep the rule true after every public call, so the second call cannot open the other side
Hold the rule only right after the constructor runs, then let mutators change the fields
options.misconception: an invariant is a construction-time promise only

options.text: Let either mutator set its flag, because a field is private and clients cannot see it
options.misconception: private fields make any stored combination legal

options.text: Let the accessor hide the second flag so the pair never looks illegal to a reader
options.misconception: reporting a safe value repairs the stored state

questions.explanation: An invariant is a claim about the object that must hold whenever control sits outside the object's own code, so every mutator has to end with the rule true. The tempting belief is that establishing the rule once in the constructor is enough, but openRight() can be called at any later moment and only that later call can restore the rule. A private field and a polite accessor change what a reader sees, not what the object stores.
questions.hint: Ask how many separate moments in an object's life a client can observe.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.learningObjective: explain why a guard written after the field write leaves a half-updated object behind
questions.stem: A method raises a stored count and only then checks the ceiling, throwing when the new count is too high. Why does the order of those two steps matter?

options.text: The field is already updated when the throw happens, so the object keeps the illegal value
The check runs on an argument the method has already overwritten by raising the count
options.misconception: an argument is changed by assigning through this

options.text: A throw inside a method always rolls back every field the method touched
options.misconception: exceptions undo earlier statements in the same method

options.text: The ceiling only matters for reads, so raising the count first is harmless
options.misconception: a rule about stored values stops mattering once written

questions.explanation: Nothing in Java undoes a completed assignment when a later statement throws, so writing first and checking second leaves the object holding the very value the check refused. The tempting answer claims exceptions roll work back, which is true of a database transaction and false of an ordinary object. Validating first keeps the object either fully old or fully new, with no half-updated state to reason about.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two steps has already changed the field when the throw escapes.

questions.learningObjective: decide which argument a constructor must check because no legal object exists before it returns
questions.stem: A ladder class must never exist with a rung count below one, and the class exposes setRungs(int). Which value has the constructor no choice about?

options.text: The rungs argument, because an object with zero rungs would break the rule from birth
Neither value, because the setter is the only place a rule about rungs belongs
options.misconception: a later setter can repair a constructor that shipped a broken object

options.text: The field's default of zero, because a constructor only assigns what it is given
options.misconception: a default value can be left in place and still be legal

options.text: Both values, because every constructor must re-check whatever the setter checks
options.misconception: a constructor must duplicate every mutator guard

questions.explanation: A client can hold a reference to a freshly constructed ladder and read it without ever calling the setter, so any value the constructor lets through becomes an observable illegal state. The tempting belief is that the setter is the natural home for the rule, but a setter only protects calls that pass through it. A constructor that refuses an illegal argument is the only way to guarantee there is no pre-repair object to leak.

questions.learningObjective: describe what two names for one object share when a write goes through either name

b names a second object holding a copy, so a's own balance stays at zero
options.misconception: assigning a reference builds a duplicate object

options.text: b names a second object, but both objects share one balance field between them
options.misconception: a copy can still share the original's storage

options.text: b names nothing usable, because only the first name may hold an object reference
options.misconception: only the variable that ran new can be used later

options.misconception: equal field values make references compare equal

options.text: It reports false, because the test compares the fields rather than the references
options.misconception: == on objects compares their stored fields

options.misconception: a rule about stored values fixes the set of allowed calls

threw with n=3

The tempting answer blames setLo, which is the mutator that does maintain the rule, and the belief that one careful mutator protects the pair is exactly what the trace disproves. A rule spanning two fields has to be re-established by every method that changes either of them.
questions.hint: Compare the body of setLo with the body of setHi.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.learningObjective: write the mutator that keeps a dependent field in step with the field it is derived from
questions.stem: A card keeps the rule that rest never exceeds the total it is counted against. class Card { int total; int rest; int used; Card(int total, int used){ this.total = total; this.used = used; this.rest = total - used; } void setUsed(int used){ this.used = used; ____ } String show(){ return used + "/" + rest; } } Card c = new Card(10, 4); c.setUsed(7); System.out.print(c.show()); Which fragment fills the blank so the program prints 7/3?

options.text: rest = total - used;
used = total - used;
options.misconception: the derived field is the one whose value gets recomputed

options.text: rest = rest - used;
options.misconception: the derived field is decremented by the new count

options.text: total = used + rest;
options.misconception: the total is rebuilt from the count and the old remainder

questions.explanation: Recomputing rest as total minus the count that was just stored puts the two fields back in step, so rest becomes 3 and show prints 7/3. The tempting fragment B rebuilds used instead, which leaves rest stale at 6 and prints 3/6, and D moves the total while rest keeps the old remainder and prints 7/6. Whenever one field is derived from another, the mutator that changes the source has to refresh the derived one inside the same call.
questions.hint: Decide which of the two fields is computed from the other.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.learningObjective: judge which statements about two references to one object are true
questions.stem: A client holds one Guard object in a local named g, copies that reference into a second local named h, and later passes g to helper methods. Which statements about that code are true?

options.text: After h = g, both names reach one object, so a write through h shows up when g is read
A method handed the object as a parameter can change the state the caller observes
After h = g, Java allocates a second object whose values then evolve apart
options.misconception: assigning a reference builds a duplicate of the object

options.text: Two objects built from equal constructor arguments stay separate, so a write to one spares the other
Because arguments are copied, a method can never change the object its caller passed in
options.misconception: copying an argument copies the object behind it

questions.explanation: A reference value is an address, so copying it adds a name without adding an object, which is why A and B both hold. C is the belief that assignment duplicates the referent, and E confuses copying the reference with copying the object, which is the same error seen from the other side. D is the useful contrast: two separate constructions make two objects, so equal arguments do not create sharing.
questions.hint: For each statement, count the objects that exist afterwards.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.learningObjective: evaluate which single change makes a capacity class keep its headroom rule true
questions.stem: A ring class is class Ring { int size; int cap; Ring(int cap){ this.cap = cap; } boolean push(int item){ if (size == cap) { return false; } cap = cap - 1; size = size + 1; return true; } int free(){ return cap; } }. With Ring q = new Ring(2); the calls q.push(1) and q.push(2) print truefalse1, so the ring refuses the second item. Which single change repairs it?

options.text: Leave cap alone in push and test size against it, so free keeps reporting headroom
Add a second field for the room left and keep shrinking cap inside push
options.misconception: the shortage is a missing field rather than a shrinking one

options.text: Return false from push whenever cap drops below one, whatever size has reached
options.misconception: a capacity value is itself the fullness test

options.text: Let size grow only on odd passes, so the two counters keep some parity
options.misconception: two counters must be advanced in step to stay consistent

questions.explanation: cap is doing two incompatible jobs, storing the size the ring was built with and reporting how much room is left, and shrinking it in push collapses the two so the very first push makes the ring look full. The tempting answers treat the symptom, a second counter or a parity rule, as the disease, but any fix that keeps shrinking cap leaves free() and the fullness test describing different quantities. One field should mean one thing, and the fullness test should compare size to an unchanging cap.
questions.hint: List every job cap is doing and decide which two conflict.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.learningObjective: judge which members belong in a class that guarantees a rule across two fields
questions.stem: A window class stores lo and hi and promises that lo is never above hi. Which members belong in such a class?

options.text: a constructor that refuses any pair whose lo is above its hi
a setLo that lifts hi to lo whenever hi would fall below it
a getHi that returns lo whenever hi is smaller, so no reader sees a bad pair
options.misconception: a safe report is the same thing as a safe stored state

options.text: a setHi that refuses any hi below the lo the object already holds
a getLo that returns hi when lo is larger, so callers never observe the bad order
options.misconception: swapping the value in the report repairs the two fields

questions.explanation: A, B and D all act on the stored fields, so each one leaves lo at or below hi for any call a client can make. C and E are the tempting pair: they make the printed or returned value look legal while the object keeps an illegal pair, which is exactly the kind of class that looks fine in a test and corrupts data later. Guaranteeing an invariant means every path that writes state has to end with the rule true, not merely every path that reports it.
questions.hint: Ask of each member whether it changes the fields or only the report.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.learningObjective: judge which changes stop a constructor from publishing a half built object
questions.stem: A constructor can hand its own reference to other code before it finishes. Which changes keep a half built object from escaping?

options.text: Validate every argument before this is registered anywhere at all
Delay adding this to shared collections until the last constructor statement
Wrap the assignments in a try block so a thrown exception cannot leave the constructor
options.misconception: catching an exception inside makes the partial object unreachable

options.text: Keep the setup in private helpers that touch only this object's own fields
Give the class a finalize method that removes the object from any registry it joined
options.misconception: finalize can undo a registration made during a failed build

questions.explanation: A, B and D all shrink the window in which another object can hold this, so a throw inside the constructor leaves nothing behind. C is the tempting one, but catching the exception inside changes who handles the failure, not whether the partial object was already published. E is worse, because a finalizer may never run and cannot undo a registration made by a constructor that failed, so the object stays reachable for the life of the program.
questions.hint: Ask of each change whether it prevents the publication or merely reacts to it.

questions.learningObjective: diagnose a mutator that leaves a reference the client kept pointing at a detached object

options.text: relabel swaps in a new object, so the reference the client kept is now detached
relabel writes through the old object, so the client's reference still sees the change
options.misconception: reassigning a field also updates the objects clients already hold

options.text: relabel cannot change which object the field holds, since fields are final here
options.misconception: a field is final unless it is written in a constructor

options.text: the client must run a constructor again before its old reference can be reused
options.misconception: a detached reference must be revived by rebuilding the object

questions.explanation: relabel assigns a different Tag to the field, so the cell now points at the new object while the client's held reference still names the old one, and the two report different codes. The tempting answer assumes the write reached through to the object the client kept, but assigning a field changes which object the field names and touches nothing inside either Tag. Any later change the client wants must go back through the cell, because its own reference now describes an object the cell has forgotten.
questions.hint: Ask how many Tag objects exist and which one the field names after the call.
